items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23
items.q: He'd teach me and show me just what to do and where to make my stops, where I make rows, where I have to beat before rows and so on.

ctx.x: A couple of them did. Now, what I've learned was through Perkins. You know how I learned in the notes, it was through Perkins. See? Yeah. He'd teach me and show me just what to do and where to make my stops, where I make rows, where I have to beat before rows and so on. See? Well, then I got onto all of that very quick.

That's the same year that Alfred went to New York. He played. He was with Durante, my son. That's right. He was with Durante. Yes, sir. We got Durante's card. His wife, he never fails sending him a Christmas card every year. And when he died, he sent him a beautiful card. Jimmy Durante? Yes. Fact. Yes. In 17, Alfred Lane was with Durante in New York in the Alamo Cafe. So how could...

items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Alfred Laine Interview, 1951-04-21
items.q: Well, the man that I first started with was Dave Perkins.

ctx.x: Well, I was doing... when I had my own band, I was doing the Spanish and American War. I had then, in the Spanish and American War, I had 35 pieces, including myself. And after that, well before that rather, I used to play music right on, play field band music in different kinds of instruments with different kinds of musicians. that is different members of different organizations that came with me. And the line of a lot of children that I used to have. Very lot of children. And brought them all in. And ever since…
Well, who is the gentleman that taught you how?

Well, the man that I first started with was Dave Perkins. And ever since Dave Perkins, I went with another guy that used to play. His name was Meade, Will Meade. He was an awful good professor. Well, now that's been some years ago. He had a cigar stand on Royal and Espenade. That's where I used to go to. He was a mighty nice musician too.

items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1964-04-25
items.q: That's the way Perkins learned us how to play.

ctx.x: Yeah. Dauphine, what was the other street that it was on? Dauphine and Lusitanus. Dauphine near what? Near Lusitanus? Lusitanus. Lusitanus. Wasn't it? No. On Dauphine and Lusitanus? Yeah, that's right. Well, that's right near Knob's Bar. Yeah, next to the police station. Where, Lusitanus? Lusitanus. Yeah. That's where we used to be. On Lusitanus. Yeah. That's where we used to be.

That's the way Perkins learned us how to play. Oh, with respect to you, bumps you the rat tail. I forgot the name. I can't figure that. He pumped away with his trombones, that damn pursuing. Boy, he turned the house down.

items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine, Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine and Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1959-02-27
items.q: Well, Lawrence Vega played with you. Yeah. And Pacquet and Dave Perkins and you, I forgot who the others were

ctx.x: Then I had another, just that quick, really. I see above the staff, Richie Brunus. Little Vega was the finest trumpet player that was in this man's town. Lawrence Vega. That kid could play a horn. Ragtime? Yeah. Yeah, Lawrence Vega. Brother, that boy, oh, he was young.

He played, that time he played with him and Pacquet and Dave Perkins. Huh. Well, Lawrence Vega played with you. Yeah. And Pacquet and Dave Perkins and you, I forgot who the others were, but anyhow, that's really, and you know Pacquet played good music. Pacquet played good music.
You heard of Ashil Pacquet playing clarinet, haven't you? He played good, he played good.
